Resource Library

Resource Library

Two hubs and a book. Insurance is everything you need working a claim; General is codes, materials and manufacturer specs. The AI Field Manual is separate — it’s about the tools, not the trade.

Cardinal Roofing & Renovations, LLC — 5735 Webster St, Dayton OH 45414 · 937.576.6753 · Admin@cardinalrenovations.net

Resource Library v3 · July 2026 · Sources: 2019 Residential Code of Ohio, 2024 Ohio Building Code, Ohio Admin. Code Title 4101:8, Ohio Admin. Code 3901-1-54, Ohio Revised Code Chapters 3901, 3951, 1345. Not legal advice.

Insurance

Working a claim — from the code you cite to the way you document the file to the way you keep yourself on the right side of ORC Ch. 3951.

General

The construction side. Code is what the roof has to meet. Manufacturer specs are what the warranty demands. Both matter on every job.

Ohio Insurance Law

How Ohio regulates the way carriers must handle roof claims. Insurance-side citations govern the claim process; construction-code citations govern the roof itself. Both matter.

Ohio Matching Regulation

OAC 3901-1-54(I)(1)(b) Insurance side

When an interior or exterior loss requires replacement of an item and the replaced item does not match the quality, color or size of the item suffering the loss, the insurer shall replace as much of the item as necessary to result in a reasonably comparable appearance.

Use it when: An adjuster is offering to replace only the damaged slope or a patch of shingles, and the discontinued shingle, faded field, or line-of-sight mismatch means the repair will not blend. Frame the argument around reasonably comparable appearance. Document with dated photos of the field vs. any test shingles from the same lot.
What limits it: Wright v. State Farm (6th Cir. 2014) held that this rule does not automatically require full-roof replacement for any mismatch. The insured must show the proposed repair would not produce a reasonably comparable appearance — not just that a mismatch exists.
partial replacementdiscontinued shingleline-of-sight

Unfair Claims Settlement Practices

ORC Chapter 3901.20 OAC 3901-1-54 (whole rule) Insurance side

Ohio prohibits carriers from misrepresenting facts or policy provisions, failing to acknowledge or act reasonably promptly on communications, refusing to pay claims without conducting a reasonable investigation, or compelling insureds to litigate to recover amounts due under the policy.

Use it when: An adjuster ignores your supplement, denies without inspecting, or delays past what's reasonable. Document every contact — date, name, what was said. A pattern of delay or non-response is the foundation for a bad-faith claim later.
Practical: Send every meaningful communication in writing (email or portal message). Verbal claims of denial are hard to enforce later; written ones are not.
bad faithdelaydenialdocumentation

Public Adjuster Licensing

ORC Chapter 3951 Insurance side

Public adjusters represent the policyholder, not the carrier, and must be licensed in Ohio. A roofer is not a public adjuster and cannot legally negotiate scope or price on the homeowner's behalf. That is the line: roofers document damage and provide their own estimate; public adjusters or attorneys negotiate with the carrier.

Use it when: A claim is stuck and you're being asked to negotiate. Refer the homeowner to a licensed public adjuster or attorney — both to protect them and to protect Cardinal from an unlicensed-practice complaint. Providing your written scope is fine. Arguing for coverage is not.
scopenegotiationreferral

Home Solicitation 3-Day Right of Rescission

ORC §1345.23(B)(2) Contract side

Contracts signed at the buyer's home for goods or services over $25 include a mandatory 3 business day right to cancel. Cardinal's roofing, siding, and window contracts include the ORC-compliant notice on the signature page and duplicate copies attached.

Use it when: Reminding a homeowner that the 3-day window has started; explaining why work cannot begin until day 4 unless the homeowner waives the right in a genuine emergency (rare and narrow).
contractcancellation

Asking for a Reinspection

A reinspection is a request that the carrier send someone back out. It is the normal next step when the first inspection produced a scope that does not match the roof, and it is the step most often skipped in favour of arguing by email.

Ask for one when:

  • The adjuster scoped from the ground, from a drone, or from an aerial report and never set foot on the slopes.
  • You were not present at the first inspection, so nothing you found is in their file.
  • A supplement was denied on the basis that the damage “is not there” — that is a factual dispute, and a factual dispute is settled by looking again.
  • Damage was found after the first visit — a leak that showed up in the next rain, decking exposed at tear-off, a slope nobody accessed.

Do not ask for one when the disagreement is about coverage or price rather than about what is physically on the building. A second person looking at the same roof does not change what the policy says.

How to ask: In writing, to the desk adjuster or the claim's assigned handler, with the claim number in the subject line. Say what specifically you want re-examined and why, attach the photographs, and propose being on site. Then follow the written request with a call — the call moves it, the writing is what exists later.
Be there. The whole point is that someone sees what you saw. Have the ladder up, the test squares still chalked if you can, and the same photographs on your phone. If the reinspection happens without you, it happens on their terms and you are back where you started.
Stay on your side of the line. Cardinal documents damage and provides its own scope. Requesting a reinspection because the physical findings are disputed is documentation work. Negotiating what the policy owes is not — that is public adjuster or attorney work under ORC Chapter 3951, and the library says so elsewhere for a reason.
reinspectionadjustersupplement

Deadlines That Actually Bite

ORC 2305.06 ORC 1311.06

Four different clocks run on a claim job, and they are not the same clock. Missing the short one costs money that the long one cannot get back.

The clocks, shortest first
ClockPeriodRuns from
Mechanic's lien — one- or two-family dwelling60 daysThe last day labour or material was furnished
Mechanic's lien — commercial75 daysSame
Serving the lien affidavit on the owner30 daysAfter the affidavit is filed
The policy's own suit-limitation clauseWhatever it saysUsually the date of loss — read it
Written contract, breach6 yearsWhen the cause of action accrues
Oral contract, breach4 yearsSame

The residential lien window is 60 days, not 75. Seventy-five is the commercial number and it is the one people quote from memory. On a house, being fifteen days late is being entirely too late.

The contract periods shortened. Ohio SB 13 cut written contracts from eight years to six and oral from six to four, effective 14 June 2021. Claims that accrued before that date run to the earlier of 14 June 2027 or whatever was left of the old eight years.

The policy's suit-limitation clause is not the statute, and it is usually shorter. A statute of limitations runs by operation of law. A suit-limitation clause is a private term inside the policy that shortens the time to sue the carrier — often to one or two years from the date of loss. Both are enforceable. Never tell a homeowner “you have six years” on the strength of the contract statute; the clause in their policy is the one that will end their claim. Read the policy, and if it is close, that is an attorney's call, not yours.
Practice: Put the last-day-of-work date in the job record on the day it happens, not from memory a month later — the 60-day clock runs from it. And note the date of loss on every claim file, because every policy deadline counts from there.
deadlineslienstatute

Construction Codes

Residential work is governed by the 2019 Residential Code of Ohio (RCO), based on the 2018 IRC. Commercial and multi-family fall under the 2024 Ohio Building Code (OBC). Municipal jurisdictions can amend either.

Residential — RCO Chapter 9

When Roof Recover is Prohibited

RCO R908.3 OAC 4101:8-9-01

A roof recover (layover) is not permitted where any of the following apply:

  • The existing roof or covering is water-soaked or has deteriorated to the point that it is not adequate as a base for additional roofing.
  • The existing covering is slate, clay, cement or asbestos-cement tile.
  • The existing roof has two or more applications of any type of roof covering.
  • Wood shingle or shake without a gypsum/mineral-fiber barrier.
Use it when: Adjuster is proposing a layover on a house with two existing layers, or partial repair on a roof with a deteriorated first layer. Code compels tear-off. This is the single biggest lever for turning a repair scope into a full-replacement scope where Ordinance & Law coverage applies.
Document: Photo the shingle edge showing layer count. Photo any water-staining, blistering, or delamination on the first layer visible from attic or lifted edge. Note visible layer count in the inspection report.
tear-off2+ layersfull replacementordinance & law

Ice Barrier Requirement

RCO R905.1.2

Ohio's Table 301.2(1) designates the entire state as an ice-forming region. An ice barrier is required on new asphalt shingle, metal shingle, mineral-surfaced roll, slate, wood shingle, and wood shake roofs. The barrier must be either two layers of underlayment cemented together, or a self-adhering polymer-modified bitumen sheet. It must extend from the eave edge to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line of the building, measured along the slope.

On roofs with slope ≥ 8:12, the barrier extends 36 inches up the slope from the eave.

Use it when: An adjuster's scope for a re-roof doesn't include ice & water membrane, or only shows a strip at the eave without the full wall-line coverage. Code requires it. Add the line item and cite R905.1.2.
Document: Note the overhang depth in inches (drip edge to exterior wall). This determines how far up the slope the barrier must extend. Include in the measurement worksheet.
ice & watereaveunderlayment

Underlayment Requirements

RCO R905.1.1 RCO Table R905.1.1(2)

Asphalt shingle underlayment must conform to ASTM D226, D4869, or D6757 (synthetic). Application depends on slope:

  • 2:12 up to < 4:12: Two layers of underlayment required (or self-adhering underlayment throughout).
  • 4:12 and steeper: One layer of underlayment required.
Use it when: Adjuster's scope shows single-layer felt on a low-slope section. Code requires double-layer or self-adhering for anything under 4:12. Common on porch roofs, dormers, and additions.
feltsyntheticlow slope

Asphalt Shingle Fastening

RCO R905.2.5

Fasteners must be galvanized steel, stainless, aluminum, or copper, minimum 12-gauge shank with a minimum 3/8-inch diameter head. Length must penetrate through the roofing material and at least 3/4 inch into the sheathing (or fully through sheathing less than 3/4 inch thick).

Minimum count: 4 nails per strip shingle in standard wind zones; 6 nails in high-wind zones (roof slope > 21:12 or where manufacturer requires it). Manufacturer's instructions may require more — the code minimum is a floor, not a ceiling.

Use it when: Documenting installation failures on the existing roof (nail placement above the seal strip, exposed nails, blow-off patterns from under-nailing). Also for defending your own scope when an adjuster tries to strip out a "high-wind installation" line item.
Document: Close-up photo of exposed nail failure, blown-off shingles showing nail count and placement. Note manufacturer of existing shingle if identifiable; call their tech line for the nailing spec.
nailswind damageinstallation defect

Drip Edge

RCO R905.2.8.5

Drip edge is required at eaves and rakes of shingle roofs. It must be corrosion-resistant metal, extend at least 1/4 inch below the sheathing, and extend back onto the roof deck a minimum of 2 inches. Adjacent segments overlap at least 2 inches. Fasten at intervals not exceeding 12 inches on center. At eaves, underlayment is installed over the drip edge; at rakes, underlayment is installed under the drip edge.

Use it when: Adjuster's scope excludes new drip edge on a full re-roof. Code requires it on every eave and rake. Legacy roofs installed before drip edge was required often lack it entirely — document that and add it as required-by-code.
A gutter apron is not a drip edge, and this section will not buy you one. Different profiles, different jobs: drip edge is the required eave and rake metal; a gutter apron has a longer back leg that carries water over the back edge of the gutter, on a house where the fascia is set back or the gutter hangs low. It is a real, billable item and often the right call — bill it as a gutter detail on its own merits. Cite R905.2.8.5 for it and an adjuster who knows the code will discount everything else you said.
drip edgegutter aproneaverake

Flashings — Step, Wall, Valley, Chimney

RCO R905.2.8 RCO R903.2

Base, cap, and step flashing must be corrosion-resistant metal, sized and installed to prevent water intrusion at wall intersections, chimneys, skylights, and roof penetrations. Step flashing at sidewalls must be a minimum of 4 inches high and 4 inches wide, integrated shingle-by-shingle, and covered by the wall covering above (siding, brick, or counter-flashing at masonry).

Use it when: Adjuster is proposing to reuse existing flashings on a re-roof, or excludes chimney counter-flashing. Reuse is functionally impossible without damaging the flashing during shingle removal; code demands new integrated flashings on new installations.
Document: Photo the existing step flashing condition (rusted, sealed with caulk, short-length, or missing entirely). Note whether counter-flashing is cut into masonry or surface-sealed.
step flashingcounter flashingchimneyreuse

Attic Ventilation

RCO R806

Enclosed attics and rafter spaces must have cross-ventilation. Minimum net free ventilation area is 1/150 of the ventilated space, reducible to 1/300 when at least 40% and not more than 50% of the ventilation is in the upper portion of the space (i.e., balanced ridge + soffit intake).

Net free area required — worked at three attic sizes
Attic floorAt 1/150At 1/300Difference
1,200 sq ft1,152 in²576 in²576 in²
1,600 sq ft1,536 in²768 in²768 in²
2,000 sq ft1,920 in²960 in²960 in²
2,400 sq ft2,304 in²1,152 in²1,152 in²

Attic square feet × 144 ÷ 150 (or ÷ 300) = required square inches of net free area, not gross vent area. NFA is printed on the vent’s data sheet and is always the smaller of the two numbers.

Use it when: Existing roof shows heat blistering, premature granule loss, or ice damming caused by inadequate ventilation. Re-roof scope should include bringing ventilation to code. Adjusters often exclude ventilation upgrades as "improvement" — the counter is that installing a non-compliant assembly on the new roof would violate code.
Document: Photo existing ventilation type (ridge, box, gable, power). Check for soffit intake — blocked or absent soffit vents are the most common defect. Note attic temperature vs outdoor if inspecting on a warm day.
ventilationridge ventsoffitice damming

Roof Decking / Sheathing

RCO R803 RCO R908.3

Sheathing must be structurally sound and capable of holding fasteners. Wood structural panels (OSB, plywood) must meet the span rating for the framing. Spaced or plank sheathing is acceptable on many older homes but limits fastener options and may require overlay. Deteriorated, delaminated, or rotted decking must be replaced before installing new roof covering — a re-cover over unsound decking is prohibited.

Use it when: Discovering rot or delamination during tear-off. Photograph before covering. Ohio code makes decking replacement a code-required scope item when the existing sheathing cannot support new roofing; Ordinance & Law coverage often pays for this even when standard coverage doesn't. Verify the homeowner's policy has O&L coverage before promising anything.
Document: Photo each section of failed decking with a tape measure or ruler in frame for scale. Log square footage replaced. Save the removed board as evidence when reasonable.
deckingrotordinance & law

Kickout & Roof-to-Wall Flashing

RCO R903.2.1

Where a sloped roof runs down into a vertical sidewall — a dormer cheek, a garage wall, a second-storey wall over a porch — the last shingle course dumps its whole slope's water at the wall. Without a diverter it runs behind the siding instead of into the gutter.

The code does not use the words “kickout flashing.” It is written as a function, and that is how you should quote it: flashings are required at wall and roof intersections, and “a flashing shall be installed to divert the water away from where the eave of a sloped roof intersects a vertical sidewall.” Metal flashing must be corrosion-resistant and not less than 0.019″ (No. 26 galvanized sheet).

Quoting the sentence beats saying “code requires a kickout” and being told the word is not in the book. It is not — the requirement still is.

Use it when: An adjuster's scope has step flashing but no diverter at the bottom of a roof-to-wall run, or a re-roof is scoped to reuse whatever is there. The flashing at the bottom of that run is the one that fails, and the damage it causes is inside the wall where nobody photographs it.
Document: Photograph every roof-to-wall termination from the ground and from the roof. Note whether a diverter exists, whether it is a formed piece or a bent shingle, and whether it discharges into the gutter or past the end of it. Then photograph the siding and trim directly below — staining, swollen trim, soft sheathing, peeling paint in a vertical stripe. That stripe is the argument.
This one is a liability, not just a line item. A missing diverter is the single most common cause of hidden wall rot behind cladding. If Cardinal re-roofs and reinstalls the same non-compliant detail, the next leak is Cardinal's. Cardinal's own gutter scope already specifies it — “install aluminum kickout flashing at all critical roof-to-wall intersections where gutters terminate” — so the roof scope should match.
kickoutroof-to-wallflashing

Slope Decides the System

RCO R905.2.2

Pitch is not a preference on a roof. It decides what may legally go on it.

What the slope permits — asphalt shingles
SlopeAsphalt shingles?Underlayment
4:12 and steeperYesSingle layer
2:12 up to 4:12YesDouble layer — RCO R905.1.1
Below 2:12No — not permittedNeeds a low-slope system, not shingles

Asphalt shingles may be used only on slopes of two units vertical in twelve horizontal (2:12) or greater. From 2:12 up to 4:12, double underlayment is required. Below 2:12 the answer is not “shingles with extra underlayment” — it is a different roof covering entirely.

In Dayton housing stock the sub-2:12 areas are porch roofs, additions, garage decks and shed dormers. They are small, they are easy to miss on an aerial report, and they are where the callback comes from.

Use it when: A porch or addition is scoped as shingles at the same unit price as the main roof. Measure the pitch before you agree. If it is under 2:12 the line item is a low-slope system and it prices differently.
Document: Pitch every plane separately, not just the main roof. A pitch gauge photo on the low plane, with the reading visible, settles the argument before it starts.
Do not sell shingles below 2:12. The code does not permit it, no manufacturer warranty covers it, and the leak is yours. If the existing roof has shingles down there, that is a defect to document — not a precedent to match.
slopelow slopeunderlayment

Powered Attic Ventilators

RCO R806

A powered attic ventilator is a fan, and a fan does not fix a ventilation deficit — it moves the problem. R806 is satisfied by net free area, balanced low-to-high: 1/150 of the ventilated space, reducible to 1/300 when 40–50% of it is in the upper portion.

Two failures come up on inspection, and both are worth photographing:

  • Paired with a ridge vent, it short-circuits. The fan pulls its air from the nearest opening, which is the ridge six feet away, not from the soffits thirty feet away. The attic barely ventilates and the ridge vent becomes an intake.
  • Starved of intake, it depressurizes the attic and pulls from the house. With soffits blocked or absent, the easiest air path is through can lights, the attic hatch and top plates — so it draws conditioned air out of the living space, and in winter it drags moisture up with it.

Intake must be at least equal to exhaust. If it is not, adding a fan makes it worse, not better.

Use it when: You find a power vent on a roof that also has a ridge vent, or a power vent over blocked soffits. Both are documentable defects. If the unit itself is hail-struck or the motor has failed, that is a covered line item on its own — but do not present the fan as the ventilation fix.
Document: Photograph the fan, the ridge line, and the soffit intake in the same walk. Note whether the thermostat/humidistat responds. Check the manufacturer's system requirements before scoping a fan alongside ridge vent — several shingle and vent warranties restrict mixing exhaust types.
power ventventilationintake
Walls — RCO Chapter 7

Water-Resistive Barrier — the Layer Behind the Siding

RCO R703.2

Every exterior wall needs a water-resistive barrier behind the cladding: one layer of No. 15 asphalt felt complying with ASTM D226 Type 1, or another approved barrier — which is what a modern house wrap is. It goes over the studs or sheathing of all exterior walls.

The lapping is written down, and it is the part that gets skipped:

  • Applied horizontally, upper course lapped over the lower by not less than 2″.
  • Where joints occur, lapped not less than 6″.
  • Continuous to the top of the wall, and terminated at penetrations and building appendages so the wall envelope still works.

Shingle-fashion is the whole idea: every lap sheds onto the one below, so water that gets past the siding runs down the barrier and back out. A wrap installed upside-down at one course, or taped instead of lapped, is a funnel.

Use it when: A siding scope is written as “siding only” with no barrier line. If the existing wall has no wrap or the wrap is torn, damaged or discontinuous, the barrier is a required part of the re-side — it is not an upgrade the homeowner is choosing.
Document: Photograph the wall once a section of siding is off — that is the only moment the barrier is visible. Note whether there is felt, a branded wrap, or nothing; whether laps run the right way; whether it is continuous behind trim and at the band board. If there is nothing behind the siding, that photo is the line item.
house wrapWRBsiding

Re-Siding Over What Is Already There

RCO R703.1

The wall has to end up as a weather-resistant exterior wall envelope — cladding, barrier, flashing and the way they meet at every opening, working as one assembly. That is the standard the finished wall is judged against, not “the new siding is nailed on.”

Which is why going over existing siding is a decision, not a shortcut. Three things decide it:

  • Can the barrier be made continuous? If the existing cladding stays, you generally cannot inspect or repair what is behind it. Damage found later is behind two layers.
  • Do the openings still integrate? Window and door flashing has to lap over the barrier and under the cladding. Adding a layer changes every jamb, sill and head detail.
  • Is the substrate sound? Soft sheathing, rot at the band board, or previous water tracking behind a kickout that was never there — all of it stays hidden if you cover it.
Use it when: An adjuster's scope prices a layover because it is cheaper, or a homeowner asks for one. Answer it on the assembly, not on price: what happens at the windows, and what happens to anything already wet.
Tear-off is the moment you find out. Scope wall repairs after exposure, never from a guess, and photograph what you find before you cover it. A wall opened, photographed and re-closed is a documented condition. A wall covered without looking is a warranty claim waiting.
re-sidelayoverflashing
Commercial — OBC Chapter 15

2024 Ohio Building Code — Chapter 15

OBC Chapter 15 OAC 4101:1

Commercial and multi-family structures fall under the Ohio Building Code (adopted from IBC 2021), administered by the Ohio Board of Building Standards. Chapter 15 (Roof Assemblies and Rooftop Structures) parallels the residential Chapter 9 but with heavier structural, drainage, and fire-resistance requirements.

Key differences from residential:

  • Class A/B/C roof covering ratings mandatory (UL 790 or ASTM E108).
  • Wind uplift resistance per ASCE 7 (FM 4470, UL 580, or Miami-Dade approval).
  • Overflow scupper or secondary drainage required.
  • Minimum 1/4:12 positive drainage on low-slope assemblies (with reroof exception per OBC 1511).
Use it when: Estimating on a commercial property (mixed-use, apartments over 3 units, retail, industrial). Insurance claims on commercial roofs go through commercial adjusters who expect commercial-code compliance and commercial documentation standards (RS Means, formal moisture surveys, roof condition reports).

Commercial Reroofing Rules

OBC 1511

Similar to residential R908, but applies to modified bitumen, TPO, EPDM, PVC, built-up, and metal panel systems. Recover is prohibited where the existing membrane is water-soaked, has two or more roof assemblies present, or where the existing insulation cannot be dried. Slate, clay, and cement tile also prohibit recover.

Use it when: Documenting flat-roof claims on light commercial or multi-family properties. Moisture surveys (infrared or capacitance) become the standard evidence rather than shingle test squares.
Miami Valley — Municipal Amendments

City of Dayton

Dayton enforces the 2019 Residential Code of Ohio through the Division of Building Services. Roof replacement typically does not require a permit if it does not involve structural work, alteration of the roof geometry, or replacement of more than 50% of the sheathing. Structural repairs, additions, or full deck replacement do require a permit.

Check with: Dayton Division of Building Services for the specific project. Local enforcement practice varies, especially in older neighborhoods where legacy structure is common. Historic-district properties may have additional review requirements.

City of Kettering

Kettering's Building Department distinguishes four re-roofing tiers, with permit and inspection required only for total replacement (defined as tear-off with more than 50% of sheathing replacement). Tear-offs without significant deck work do not require a permit but must still comply with the RCO. Applications and inspections are handled through the online portal.

tier systemonline portal

Huber Heights

Huber Heights enforces the 2019 RCO. Roofing permits are required for full replacements with structural work; simple tear-off/recover generally does not require a permit but must be code-compliant. Reach out to the Huber Heights Division of Development for project-specific determination.

Other Miami Valley Jurisdictions

Beavercreek, Centerville, Springboro, Moraine, Trotwood, West Carrollton, and Vandalia all enforce the RCO with similar local variance around permit thresholds. As a rule for the region:

  • Simple tear-off and re-cover with matching materials generally does not require a permit.
  • Any structural work — rafters, trusses, dormers, deck replacement over 50% — requires a permit.
  • Historic-district or overlay-zoned properties require review before work begins.
Practice: Call the AHJ (Authority Having Jurisdiction) before signing the contract if there's any doubt. A denied permit mid-job costs more than a five-minute phone call.

County vs. Municipality — Who Actually Has Jurisdiction

The cards above name cities. Not every Cardinal address is in one.

Ohio addresses carry a mailing city that is frequently not the authority having jurisdiction. A house with a Dayton or Centerville postal address can sit in a township, in unincorporated county land, or inside a different municipality altogether — and the permit office changes with it, not with the envelope.

The rule that holds: an incorporated municipality that operates its own building department issues its own permits and does its own inspections. Everywhere else — townships and unincorporated land — the county building department is the authority. Which is why the three largest jurisdictions on this page have their own cards and the rest of the region does not: they are not the same office.

Do not infer the AHJ from the mailing address, and do not infer it from this card. The only reliable way to know is to ask, using the parcel — not the street name. Pull the parcel on the county auditor's site, get the taxing district off it, and call the office that district points to. Five minutes before the contract is signed; a stopped job and a re-inspection fee afterwards.
Use it when: The address is outside a named city on this page, or the homeowner says “we're Dayton” and the parcel says a township. Confirm the office before you promise a permit timeline to anyone.
Record it on the job: the AHJ you confirmed, who you spoke to, and the date. The next rep on that street should not have to make the call again.

Policy Provisions

Three coverages that turn a partial claim into a full one. Check the declarations page and endorsements before making any promises.

Ordinance & Law Coverage

Usually a built-in Additional Coverage on HO-3 policies, commonly capped at a percentage of Coverage A, with higher limits available by endorsement. It is not one of the lettered coverages. Pays for costs incurred to bring the property into current code compliance as part of a covered loss. Without it, the carrier only owes the pre-loss condition — code-required upgrades come out of the homeowner's pocket.

Check for: percentage of Coverage A dwelling amount (10%, 25%, 50%), or a flat dollar limit. Some policies exclude it entirely, some include it automatically. If absent, decking replacement and ventilation upgrades required by code become the homeowner's cost.

RCV vs ACV Settlement

Replacement Cost Value: carrier pays the full cost to replace with like kind and quality, minus deductible. Depreciation is initially withheld and released upon completion of the work.

Actual Cash Value: carrier pays RCV minus depreciation. Depreciation is not recoverable.

Common trap: A roof-age endorsement can convert an otherwise-RCV policy to ACV on the roof specifically after a certain roof age (often 15 or 20 years). Homeowner may not know this. Read the endorsement pages, not just the declarations.

Matching Endorsement

Some carriers offer an optional endorsement that expands the state matching regulation and explicitly requires uniform-appearance repairs including full replacement of undamaged sections when necessary. Others explicitly limit matching to a single slope or single side of a wall.

Check for: "matching," "uniform appearance," "cosmetic" language in the policy schedule and any endorsements. Some carriers add a cosmetic-damage exclusion that specifically strips matching for hail spatter without functional damage.
The Money
These worked examples are examples. The numbers below are made up to show the order the arithmetic runs in. Depreciation schedules, roof life expectancy and whether labor is depreciated are set by the carrier and vary policy to policy — none of them is Ohio law. Read the declarations page and the endorsements before you put a number in front of a homeowner.

Coverage A, B, C, D — which one pays for what

A homeowner asks “is this covered?” The answer is usually “under which coverage?” On a standard HO-3 the roof is Coverage A, the detached garage is Coverage B, and the ruined furniture underneath the leak is Coverage C.

The four coverages on a standard homeowner policy
CoveragePays forOn a storm claim
A — DwellingThe house and what is attached to itRoof, siding, gutters, attached porch
B — Other StructuresDetached structures on the lotDetached garage, shed, fence. Typically 10% of Coverage A, with its own limit
C — Personal PropertyContentsWhat the leak ruined inside
D — Loss of UseAdditional living expenseRarely reached on a roof claim

Ordinance or Law is where code-upgrade money lives, and it is not one of the four lettered coverages. On a standard HO-3 the letters stop at D. Code-upgrade cost comes from a separate Additional Coverage built into the form — commonly capped at 10% of Coverage A — with higher limits available by endorsement. Some proprietary forms reduce or exclude it. This is what pays for what the Ohio Residential Code requires on a reroof but the old roof did not have, such as ice barrier, drip edge and fastening upgrades. Find the limit on the schedule before you write the supplement, and do not assume it is absent just because no endorsement is listed.

Rentals are a different form. Landlord policies are usually dwelling-fire (DP) forms, where the letters run further — D is Fair Rental Value and E is Additional Living Expense. Confirm the form number at the top of the declarations page before you quote a letter.

Use it: when the adjuster's scope only lists the house, ask whether the detached garage was inspected. It is a separate coverage with its own limit, and it is one of the easiest things to leave off a scope.

Flat deductible vs percentage deductible

A flat deductible is a dollar figure. A percentage deductible is a percentage of Coverage A — not of the claim — and on a wind or hail loss it is often larger than the all-perils deductible on the same policy.

What a wind/hail percentage costs at four dwelling amounts
Coverage A1%2%5%
$200,000$2,000$4,000$10,000
$300,000$3,000$6,000$15,000
$400,000$4,000$8,000$20,000
$500,000$5,000$10,000$25,000

Straight arithmetic, not a carrier's schedule. The percentage and the Coverage A figure both come off the declarations page.

Get this before you quote anything: a photo of the declarations page showing Coverage A, the all-perils deductible and the separate wind/hail deductible. A homeowner who thinks their deductible is $1,000 when the policy says 2% of $350,000 — that is $7,000 — is a signed job that dies at the kitchen table.

The order the money arrives in

Example numbers. The 25-year roof life, the straight-line schedule and whether labor is depreciated are assumptions used here to show the order the arithmetic runs in. All three are set by the carrier and the policy — none is Ohio law.

On an RCV policy the carrier pays in stages — at least twice, and more if the scope is supplemented. The first check is the actual cash value minus the deductible. The rest — the recoverable depreciation — is released after the work is done and documented. The release is capped at what the job actually cost: if the final invoice comes in under the approved scope, the carrier releases the lower figure. The withheld amount is a ceiling, not a guaranteed payment.

Worked example — RCV policy, 1% wind/hail on $340,000, roof aged 14 of an assumed 25-year life
StepAmount
Replacement cost of the approved scope$21,450.00
Less depreciation withheld (14 of 25 years = 56%)−$12,012.00
Actual cash value$9,438.00
Less wind/hail deductible (1% of $340,000)−$3,400.00
First check$6,038.00
Depreciation released on completion (up to the amount actually incurred)$12,012.00
Total the carrier pays$18,050.00
Homeowner pays the deductible$3,400.00

$18,050 + $3,400 = $21,450. On a clean full-RCV settlement the carrier plus the homeowner equals the job. It legitimately will not close when the estimate carries non-recoverable depreciation, an ACV roof endorsement, a sublimit or a cap. If it does not close, ask the adjuster which of those applies before you assume something was left out — there is usually a line on the estimate that says.

Say it like this: “The insurance company pays for the approved scope minus your deductible, and they pay it in two parts — some now, the rest when the work is finished. Your deductible is your part. If the carrier hasn’t approved everything yet, or if your policy has a roof payment schedule on it, your share can be more than the deductible — I’ll check your declarations page and endorsements and tell you before you sign anything.”

Why the first check is small — and why $0 is not a denial

Example numbers. The 25-year roof life, the straight-line schedule and whether labor is depreciated are assumptions used here to show the order the arithmetic runs in. All three are set by the carrier and the policy — none is Ohio law.

When the approved scope is larger than the deductible but the actual cash value is not, the first check is zero and the claim is still approved. It is not denied, and the recoverable depreciation is owed on completion. What the homeowner has is a timing problem, not a coverage problem.

Check which zero it is. Compare the replacement cost of the scope to the deductible, not the ACV. If replacement cost is above the deductible — as in the table below — the balance comes on completion. If the whole replacement cost is below the deductible, there is no payment now and none later, and that is a dead end rather than a timing problem. Make that comparison before you tell anyone a second check is coming.

Worked example — same $21,450 scope, a roof aged 21 of an assumed 25-year life, 2% deductible on $340,000
StepAmount
Replacement cost$21,450.00
Less depreciation (21 of 25 years = 84%)−$18,018.00
Actual cash value$3,432.00
Less deductible (2% of $340,000)−$6,800.00
First check — floored at zero$0.00
Released on completion$14,650.00
Total the carrier pays$14,650.00
Homeowner pays the deductible$6,800.00

The check is floored at zero, but the deductible is not forgiven — the part it could not absorb comes off the release instead. On this policy, with the work completed and all of the depreciation recoverable, the carrier's total comes to replacement cost minus the deductible: $21,450 − $6,800 = $14,650, and the homeowner's share is the full $6,800. If the work is never finished nothing is released and the carrier's total stays at the first check; where a roof payment schedule endorsement applies it does not work this way at all — see The roof payment schedule endorsement.

Use it: a homeowner who gets a $0 check usually believes the claim was denied and stops answering the phone. Show them this before the check arrives, not after — and have the answer to “so how do I pay for this now?” ready, because on this example they are carrying the job until the release arrives.

Recoverable depreciation and how it is released

Depreciation withheld on an RCV policy is usually recoverable — the carrier owes it once the work is actually done, and it is released against proof, not against a phone call. Check the estimate first: many carriers print recoverable and non-recoverable depreciation as separate lines, and the non-recoverable figure is never released. Read the summary page and quote the recoverable number, not the total withheld.

  • Final invoice showing the work performed and the amount charged.
  • Completion photographs, usually including the finished roof and the disposal.
  • A certificate of completion or signed satisfaction form on some carriers.
  • Any permit close-out the jurisdiction requires.
Watch the clock. Most policies put a time limit on claiming recoverable depreciation, commonly measured from the date of loss. The limit is in the policy, not in state law, and it varies — find it on the claim, write it on the job, and do not let a job sit unfinished past it.
Common trap: a supplement approved after the ACV check has its own depreciation withheld too. Getting a supplement approved is not the same as getting it paid — the release still has to be requested on completion.

The roof payment schedule endorsement

Several carriers now attach an endorsement that converts roof surfacing from replacement cost to a scheduled payout based on the roof's age — sometimes a table of percentages by year, sometimes a flat conversion to ACV after a stated age.

When it applies, there is no recoverable depreciation to release on the roof surfacing — the scheduled amount is the whole payment for that part, and the homeowner covers the rest. The rest of the claim is unaffected: siding, gutters and interior damage normally stay on replacement cost with depreciation still recoverable. Read the endorsement for what it counts as “roof surfacing” — forms differ on whether flashing, decking and underlayment are inside or outside that word.

Find it before the inspection. It has different names on different forms — roof surfacing payment schedule, roof surfaces extended coverage, actual cash value loss settlement windstorm or hail losses to roof surfacing. It is in the endorsement pages, not on the declarations summary.
Why it matters commercially: the job is the same job, but the homeowner's share is much larger. Find it early, price it honestly, and do not let it surface after the contract is signed.
Getting Paid

Duties after loss — the homeowner's side of the contract

Every policy lists what the insured must do after a loss. Miss them and the carrier gains an argument it did not have to earn. In broad terms they run to: give prompt notice, protect the property from further damage, cooperate with the investigation, and provide records the carrier asks for.

Cardinal's part: the mitigation duty is the one a contractor can discharge for the homeowner. A tarp, dated and photographed, is evidence that the duty was met. Bill it as a line item and keep the photograph.
Read the actual policy language. The list above is the general shape, not a quotation. Some forms require a signed sworn proof of loss on request and set a deadline for it; some set a time limit for suit against the carrier. Both are in the policy, both are enforceable, and neither is something to learn about late.

The duties run both ways. Ohio’s unfair claims settlement practices rules put the carrier on its own timelines for acknowledging and acting on a claim — see Unfair Claims Settlement Practices on the Ohio Insurance Law page. Do not quote a number of days from memory.
A sworn proof of loss is the homeowner’s sworn document. Do not prepare it, do not fill it in, and never sign one for a homeowner. Hand them your estimate and your photographs — what they swear to is theirs.

The mortgage company is on the check

If there is a mortgage, the lender is almost always a named payee on the structure portion of the claim — the Coverage A and B money. Contents and loss-of-use checks normally go to the homeowner alone. The homeowner cannot simply sign the structure check over — the lender endorses it, and above a threshold it goes into a loss-draft escrow and is released in stages against inspections.

A typical loss-draft sequence — shape only, every servicer differs
StageWhat the servicer usually wants
Open the claim fileThe check, the adjuster's scope, the contractor's contract and W‑9
First releaseOften a portion up front on a signed contract
Progress releaseAn inspection, sometimes by a third party the servicer sends
Final releaseCompletion inspection, final invoice, lien waiver

Thresholds, staging and paperwork are set by the servicer, not by the carrier and not by Ohio law. Ask the homeowner to call the number on their mortgage statement and ask for the loss draft department. Loan status matters more than paperwork: if the loan is behind or in foreclosure, many servicers will not release monitored funds at all, or will apply them to the balance. No completion package fixes that, so find out early whether the homeowner is current.

Why jobs stall here: the money exists, the homeowner has the check, and nobody told them a bank has to endorse it. Ask on the first visit whether there is a mortgage. It changes the payment schedule, not the price.

Appraisal — the disagreement clause about amount

Most property policies contain an appraisal clause. Either side may invoke it when they disagree about the amount of the loss. Each side names an appraiser, the two appraisers select an umpire, and an award agreed by any two of the three is binding as to amount. The clause usually runs on deadlines — a set period to name an appraiser after a written demand, a further period for the two to agree an umpire, and a court appointment if they cannot. Read the days off the policy in front of you; they differ between forms.

Appraisal decides amount, not coverage. If the carrier says the damage is not storm damage at all, that is a coverage dispute and appraisal is the wrong tool. Read the clause on the policy in front of you — who may invoke it, what it costs, and what it binds are all in that paragraph and they differ between forms.
Where a contractor stands: Cardinal documents, scopes and prices. Explaining what the clause is, is fine. Negotiating the claim on the homeowner's behalf crosses into public adjusting, which Ohio licenses — see Public Adjuster Licensing on the Ohio Insurance Law page. Invoking appraisal is the policyholder's decision and not one to recommend: if they ask whether they should, refer them to their own attorney or a licensed public adjuster. Whether Cardinal may serve as the homeowner's named appraiser under the clause is a separate and less settled question — ask Theo, do not decide it on a driveway.

The deductible is the homeowner's to pay

ORC §2913.47Insurance side

Inflating an invoice, writing a second set of paperwork, or otherwise misstating the price of the job so the carrier absorbs the homeowner's deductible puts a false figure in front of the insurer. In Ohio, presenting a statement in support of an insurance claim — with purpose to defraud, or knowing you are facilitating a fraud — knowing that the statement is false or deceptive is a criminal offense under ORC 2913.47. Cardinal invoices the real price, every time.

Separately, Cardinal does not advertise, offer or agree to waive, absorb or rebate a deductible in any form. Whether a particular arrangement is itself unlawful in Ohio turns on the facts and on statutes outside 2913.47 — a question for Cardinal's attorney, not for a rep on a driveway.

The safe sentence: “Your deductible is your part of the job. We can't cover it, and any contractor offering to isn't doing you a favor — it's the same paperwork that gets a claim reopened.”
This card describes why Cardinal will not do it. It is not a legal opinion about anyone else. Whether a particular arrangement crosses ORC 2913.47, whether Ohio has a contractor-specific deductible statute, and how the Consumer Sales Practices Act applies to roofing advertising are questions for Cardinal's attorney. Do not accuse a competitor of a crime on a driveway.

Documentation Checklist

Photos, notes, and paper that make or break a claim. The adjuster reads what's in the file — make sure the file says what you mean.

Per-Inspection Documentation Standard

Every insurance inspection should include:

  • Ground shots of all elevations — establishes property identity, general condition.
  • Shingle layer count — edge photo showing visible layers.
  • Test square — chalked 10x10 for hail, hit count per slope.
  • Damage close-ups — ruler or coin in frame for scale.
  • Ventilation type & condition — ridge, box, gable, power. Soffit intake status.
  • Flashing condition — step, wall, chimney, skylight, pipe boots.
  • Gutter line — downspouts for granule accumulation.
  • Attic access — decking from below, insulation depth, ventilation from inside, active leaks.
  • Related property damage — siding, screens, HVAC, gutters, fascia, soffit, downspouts. Photograph even if not this claim's scope.
  • Date & time stamp on all photos.

Photo Templates by Damage Type

Hail:

  • One overall of each slope from ground.
  • One chalked 10×10 test square per slope with hit count written on chalk or paper card in frame.
  • Close-up of representative impact showing fractured mat, granule displacement, and matted circular pattern — ruler in frame for scale.
  • Ridge/hip cap close-up if impacted — hail rounds often show best on ridges.
  • Soft metals for corroboration: gutter, downspout elbow, vent hood, cap flashing, HVAC fins, screens, garage door.

Wind:

  • Missing shingle areas photographed with something for scale.
  • Lifted/creased shingles — from the side showing the crease line.
  • Seal strip failure — underside of lifted shingle showing broken seal.
  • Ridge cap displacement patterns.
  • Overall pattern shot showing directional damage consistent with wind vector.

Water intrusion (from a storm event):

  • Interior ceiling staining with dated photo.
  • Attic sheathing staining, streak marks, mold.
  • Insulation compression at leak locations.
  • Corresponding exterior condition — failed flashing, missing shingle, damaged boot.
Use it when: Building a claim file for supplement or appraisal. Adjusters weigh volume and pattern; a scattershot of impacts across slopes tells a very different story than three lonely photos.

Paper Trail

  • Copy of policy declarations page — note coverage limits, deductible, RCV vs ACV, Ordinance & Law coverage limit.
  • Sworn statement in proof of loss (if requested).
  • Cardinal's written scope with line-item pricing.
  • Adjuster's scope (Xactimate, Symbility, or PDF).
  • Line-by-line comparison — every discrepancy noted with photo or code cite.
  • Every written communication with the adjuster — email chain, portal messages.

The Punch Walk

Everything in this library up to here is about getting the job. This is the part that decides whether you get the next one.

Walk the job the day the crew finishes, before the dumpster leaves, with the homeowner if they will come. What you are looking for is not craftsmanship in the abstract — it is the specific short list of things that generate callbacks:

The punch walk, in order
WhereWhat generates the callback
Ground, all elevationsNails in the grass and beds. Magnetic sweep twice, including the driveway and any gravel. Trampled plantings, gouged siding, dented gutters from the tear-off
GuttersDebris left in the trough. Dents from ladders or bundles. Downspouts re-hung and draining away
Eaves and rakesDrip edge straight and continuous. Starter course correct. No exposed fasteners
Roof-to-wallDiverter installed and discharging into the gutter. Step flashing under the cladding, not caulked over it
PenetrationsNew boots, not re-used. Collars seated. Vents sitting flat and not shimmed with shingle scrap
RidgeCap straight and fastened, ridge vent continuous, ends closed off
InteriorNothing shaken loose. Ceilings, light fixtures, anything on shelves in the garage
Use it when: Every job, on the last day. The Production board already carries a shared punch list — put what you find on it while you are standing there, not from the truck an hour later. An item written on site with a photo gets fixed; an item remembered later gets argued about.
Document: Photograph the finished roof from all elevations the same way you photographed the damage. That set is the before-and-after, and it is what answers a complaint six months out.
punch listclose outquality

Closing the Job on Paper

The physical work being finished and the job being closed are two different events, and the money lives in the gap between them.

What has to exist before this job is done:

  • Final invoice matching the approved scope, with any supplements shown as supplements rather than folded silently into the total.
  • Certificate of completion where the carrier or the mortgage servicer requires one to release funds — the library's depreciation card covers what that release needs.
  • Lien waiver, where one is being exchanged for payment.
  • Warranty registration with the manufacturer. An unregistered system warranty is a marketing claim, not a warranty — and on the Big-3 programmes the registration window is finite.
  • Completion photographs, filed against the job, not left on somebody's phone.
  • Permit close-out where a permit was pulled. That is the jurisdiction's business, on the jurisdiction's timetable, and it is not the carrier's process.
Do not let the last-day-of-work date go unrecorded. It starts the 60-day residential mechanic's lien clock, and it is the one date nobody writes down at the time because the job feels finished. Record it the day it happens.
Use it when: The crew is off the job and the file is about to go quiet. Everything on this list is easier on the day than it is in a month, and two of them — warranty registration and the lien date — get harder or impossible with time.
close outinvoicewarranty

Claim Tips

The most common adjuster shortcuts and the code cite that answers each. Plus patterns we see from specific carriers — not accusations, just field observations to prepare for.

Claim Scenarios

“We'll only pay for the damaged slope”

Adjuster acknowledges wind or hail damage but scopes only the affected slope, leaving the other slopes with the original shingles.

Answer:
  • If shingle line is discontinued or field is significantly weathered, cite OAC 3901-1-54(I)(1)(b) — reasonably comparable appearance.
  • Document color-match failure with photos of a manufacturer sample vs field shingles under matched lighting.
  • If the roof has 2+ layers, cite RCO R908.3 — recover is prohibited, so partial replacement on top of the existing bottom layer is not code-compliant either.

“Just layer new shingles over the existing”

Adjuster proposes an overlay to save money.

Answer:
  • Count the layers. If two or more, cite RCO R908.3 — recover is not permitted.
  • If first layer is water-damaged, cite same section — unsuitable base prohibits recover regardless of layer count.
  • Point out that a code violation is a policy problem for the carrier: the homeowner would be occupying a non-code-compliant structure funded by the claim.

“Decking replacement is not covered”

Deteriorated decking is discovered during tear-off. Adjuster wants to exclude it as maintenance.

Answer:
  • If the policy has Ordinance & Law coverage, deck replacement required by code is covered under that coverage even if not covered by dwelling coverage.
  • Cite RCO R908.3 and R803 — recovering over unsound sheathing is prohibited.
  • Photograph every replaced board with scale, log square footage, submit as supplement with dated photos.
  • Check the policy declarations page before promising O&L coverage — not every homeowner has it.

“A strip of ice & water at the eave is enough”

Adjuster's scope includes ice & water at the drip edge only, not the full 24-inch-past-wall-line coverage.

Answer:
  • Cite RCO R905.1.2 — the barrier must extend from the eave edge to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line, measured along the slope.
  • Measure the overhang depth: eave-to-wall distance plus 24 inches gives you the required coverage measured up the slope.
  • Slope 8:12 or steeper needs 36 inches up the slope minimum.

“Reuse the existing flashings”

Common on step flashings, chimney counter-flashings, and skylight kits.

Answer:
  • Cite RCO R905.2.8 — flashings must be sized and installed to prevent water intrusion. Reused flashings damaged during tear-off do not satisfy this requirement.
  • Photograph the existing condition to preempt the argument: rust, caulk-sealed joints, missing counter-flashing on masonry, undersized step flashing.
  • New skylight flashing kit is standard scope on any re-roof; the skylight manufacturer's warranty typically requires new flashing with any new roof.

“Ventilation upgrade is a betterment”

Adjuster excludes new ridge vent, soffit intake, or box vent replacement as an improvement not caused by the loss.

Answer:
  • If the existing ventilation is out of compliance with RCO R806 (1/150 or 1/300 balanced), reinstalling the same non-compliant system on a code-triggered re-roof is a code violation.
  • Ordinance & Law coverage applies if the policy includes it.
  • If the existing system was itself damaged by the storm (ridge cap blown off, box vent housing hail-struck), that alone is covered damage regardless of code.

“It's just wear and tear”

Adjuster denies hail damage as normal aging or wear, or claims granule loss is not impact-related.

Answer:
  • Document impact patterns with the HAAG-style test square (a chalked 10-foot square, count of hits per slope).
  • Document circular, offset, or spatter patterns distinguishing hail from mechanical or manufacturing defects.
  • For an aged roof that also has hail impact, granule loss at impact sites (fractured mat under the impact) is diagnostic of storm damage. Photograph in raking light.
  • Brittleness test on a cool day is more reliable than on hot; document date and temperature.
  • Request the carrier's engineer report if damage is denied on that basis.

“Roof is too old for full replacement value”

Adjuster settles on Actual Cash Value only, or applies a roof-age depreciation schedule that reduces the payment significantly.

Answer:
  • Check the policy: does it pay Replacement Cost Value (RCV) with recoverable depreciation, or ACV only? If RCV, the homeowner recovers depreciation upon completion of the work.
  • If ACV only (common on older roofs under some HO-3 endorsements), the recoverable depreciation is not available. Advise the homeowner in writing.
  • Depreciation schedules can be challenged if they exceed the actual condition. A roof rated at 30 years and depreciated at 25 years remaining useful life may be challenged if it was maintained and shows better condition.
Carrier-Specific Patterns

State Farm — Engineer Reports on Denials

Pattern: On disputed hail claims, especially where the initial adjuster acknowledges damage, State Farm frequently orders an independent engineer inspection whose report concludes wear-and-tear or normal aging rather than storm impact.

Prepare for it by:
  • Documenting extensively on the first inspection with test squares, dated raking-light close-ups, and matched-lighting field photos.
  • Reviewing the engineer report for methodology — date of inspection vs. storm date, weather at inspection, whether the engineer actually walked the roof or used photos.
  • Rebuttal via independent engineer or licensed public adjuster on high-value claims.

Allstate — Cosmetic Damage Endorsement

Pattern: Some Allstate HO-3 policies (increasingly, on renewals) include a cosmetic-damage exclusion for hail impact on roofing and metals when the damage does not affect functional performance. Under this endorsement, spatter marks on shingles, dented caps and vents, and minor bruising can be excluded even when clearly caused by hail.

Answer:
  • Read the declarations page carefully — the endorsement is often an add-on that's easy to miss.
  • Document functional impact separately from cosmetic: granule loss, mat exposure, seal-strip failure, reduced service life.
  • If the roof is otherwise near end of life, cosmetic exclusion + age depreciation can gut the claim; advise the homeowner honestly.

Third-Party Administrators & Preferred Networks

Pattern: Some carriers (Erie, Nationwide, others) use third-party administrators or "preferred contractor" networks whose scopes tend to run below fair-market pricing and whose supplements go to a specific approver rather than the original adjuster. Contractors outside the network are asked to match TPA pricing.

Answer:
  • Homeowners are not obligated to use the preferred network. Cardinal's price is Cardinal's price.
  • Document with local material and labor comparables. Regional RS Means, Xactimate published rates, and manufacturer MSRPs are all cite-able.
  • If the TPA declines a supplement without inspection, that's a bad-faith foundation — escalate to the carrier direct.

Aggressive Depreciation Schedules

Pattern: Some carriers apply steep age-based depreciation to roofs at 10–15 years despite the roof being maintained and in serviceable condition. Recoverable-depreciation withholdings can approach 50% of RCV in extreme cases.

Answer:
  • Depreciation is not automatic — it should reflect actual remaining useful life.
  • Photograph the pre-loss condition of the roof to establish the depreciation baseline.
  • Cite the manufacturer's original service-life rating (30-year, 50-year architectural) as a ceiling; carrier can't depreciate faster than the roof's rated life.

Do & Don't

Field practices on the left. Ways this goes sideways on the right. Print or screenshot for the truck.

✅ DO

Read the policy first

Declarations, endorsements, limits, deductibles — before you scope, before you make promises. What's covered on the paper is what matters, not what feels fair.

Document everything on the first visit

Layer count, ventilation, flashings, decking from the attic, damage close-ups with scale, related property. Second trips are how details get missed and how adjusters get a foothold to argue the claim.

Cite specific code sections

“RCO R908.3” lands harder than “code says.” Adjusters respect precision; homeowners trust it. Keep the citations from the Construction Codes page handy in the truck.

Write a defensible scope

Every line item ties back to a code section, documented damage, or a manufacturer requirement. If you can't defend it, don't put it in. A tight, honest scope beats an inflated one on appraisal every time.

Communicate in writing

Email, portal, text with timestamps. Verbal denials and verbal approvals both disappear when the claim gets contested. Written ones do not.

Meet the adjuster on the roof

Being physically present when the adjuster inspects changes the conversation. You can point to the damage; they can't ignore what they've seen. If they show up without you, they're documenting on their terms.

Refer when the claim needs it

Public adjuster or attorney for negotiation over coverage. It protects the homeowner from a bad settlement and it protects Cardinal from unlicensed-practice risk under ORC Ch. 3951.
❌ DON'T

Waive or absorb the deductible

Ohio doesn't have a specific anti-rebating statute, but waiving a homeowner's deductible on an insurance-paid job is an unfair business practice and can be treated as fraud. Some carriers require proof of deductible payment before releasing recoverable depreciation.

Rely on Assignment of Benefits

AOBs transfer the homeowner's right to receive payment to the roofer. Ohio recognizes them but carriers have grown resistant and some policies now include anti-AOB provisions. Get legal advice before adopting AOBs as standard practice.

Inflate the scope

Every line item should be defensible with a code cite, manufacturer requirement, or documented damage. Adding items that don't clear that bar invites the carrier to reject the whole supplement and can invite fraud allegations.

Negotiate the claim yourself

Roofers document damage and provide their own scope. Roofers do not tell the adjuster what the carrier should pay, argue coverage under the policy, or represent the homeowner in settlement. That's public-adjuster or attorney work under ORC Ch. 3951.

Truck Cheat Sheet

One-card summary for the field. Prints on a single page. Take it in the truck.

Cardinal One-Page Field Card

The three levers for full replacement:

  • 2+ layers → RCO R908.3 forbids recover.
  • Deteriorated first layer → RCO R908.3 forbids recover.
  • Shingle discontinued → OAC 3901-1-54(I)(1)(b) requires reasonably comparable appearance.

Code-required scope adjusters try to strip out:

  • Ice barrier 24″ past wall line — RCO R905.1.2
  • New drip edge on all eaves/rakes — RCO R905.2.8.5
  • New step/counter flashing — RCO R905.2.8
  • Ventilation to 1/300 balanced — RCO R806
  • Double underlayment on < 4:12 slope — RCO R905.1.1
  • 4-nail (or 6 in high-wind) fastening — RCO R905.2.5

Ordinance & Law coverage: check the declarations page and the endorsement pages. Percentage of Coverage A. Pays for code-driven upgrades. If it's not there, decking replacement is on the homeowner.

Documentation minimums: ground of all elevations, layer count at edge, test square per slope, damage close-ups with scale, ventilation type & condition, flashing condition, attic if accessible, dated on every photo.

The line you don't cross: Cardinal documents damage and provides its own scope. Cardinal does not negotiate coverage under the policy. That's public adjuster or attorney work — ORC Chapter 3951.

Manufacturer Guidelines

Manufacturer installation specs are cite-able the same way code is. They set nailing patterns, starter and ridge requirements, ventilation ratios, and do-not-mix rules that govern warranty validity. When an adjuster strips out an accessory line item, the manufacturer's system-warranty spec is often the answer.

The specific do-not-mix language, current nailing patterns, and system-warranty accessory requirements for each manufacturer will be populated from the PDFs Theo is uploading. Until then, the cards below capture the general structure — program tiers, product lines, warranty names — but not the authoritative technical spec language you'd cite in a supplement or homeowner conversation.

To fill this in: upload the OC, GAF, and CertainTeed installation guides / do-not-mix documents you have. Each manufacturer's current PDF gets a card with exact quotes, section numbers, and effective dates so the citations are precise.
Cross-Cutting Rules

Class 4 Impact-Resistant — Insurance Premium Discounts

Shingles rated Class 4 under UL 2218 (the steel ball impact test) qualify for premium discounts on homeowner's insurance with most Ohio carriers — typically 10–30% off the wind/hail portion of the policy. The discount is per-carrier and requires the roofer to provide certification of Class 4 rating.

Use it when: Quoting a re-roof after a hail event. If the homeowner's carrier has the discount, upgrading to Class 4 often pays for itself over the depreciation window. Available in all three major lines: OC Duration FLEX, GAF Timberline AS II, CertainTeed Landmark IR.
UL 2218Class 4insurance discount

System Warranty Prerequisites

Every manufacturer's top-tier warranty (Golden Pledge, Platinum Protection, SureStart PLUS) requires that the full accessory kit come from the same manufacturer — starter, underlayment, hip & ridge, leak barrier, and often ventilation. Mixing brands typically drops coverage back to the standard material warranty (which is much weaker on labor).

Use it when: Defending accessory line items in a scope. If the homeowner has a system warranty on the current roof, replacing with mixed components voids that coverage. If Cardinal is offering a system warranty on the new roof, the whole accessory kit is not optional — it's a warranty prerequisite. Adjusters often try to strip starter, ridge, or underlayment lines; this is the answer.
Document: Photo the existing warranty registration paperwork if available. Note which manufacturer's system is being installed in the scope. Save receipts for accessory components as part of the job file.
accessory kitstarterridge capwarranty

Enhanced Fastening / High-Wind Installation

Beyond the RCO minimum of 4 nails per shingle, most manufacturers require 6 nails for high-wind installations and for the enhanced-warranty programs. The nail zone is above the seal strip and clearly marked on modern shingles (LayerLock on GAF, SureNail on OC).

Use it when: Adjuster strips out a "high-wind installation" line item. Answer with (a) the code minimum in the fastening code card, and (b) the manufacturer's requirement for the specific product line being installed. When the shingle is a premium product with an enhanced warranty, 6-nail is not upgrade — it's spec.
6-nailhigh windenhanced warranty

Main lines: TruDefinition Duration (standard architectural), Duration Storm (SBS-modified impact-resistant), Duration FLEX (Class 4 UL 2218). All feature the SureNail reinforced nail zone — a fabric strip that gives the fastener double-thickness engagement and makes the 6-nail installation the manufacturer default for most enhanced warranties.
